extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate or general readers of American government and public policy (students of American Government and Politics)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook guidance on federal and state policies for conserving natural resources (water, minerals, forests, waterways, water-power) and principles/practices for governing U.S. territories (organized and insular). Summarizes legal measures, administrative practices, and policy recommendations from the early 20th century.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government reclamation projects for irrigation and settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Reclamation Service (Dept. of the Interior) constructs reservoirs, drains, canals, etc., enabling settlers to draw water by ditches to irrigate farms (examples: large projects, Shoshone dam over 300 feet; six years of work made 767,958 acres fit for settlement, 424,549 irrigated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National (federal) implementation of large-scale irrigation/reclamation projects is appropriate; such projects may require high-order engineering skill and can convert barren waste to arable land. Work is largely done by government (sometimes by contract).

rubrics_metrics.name: State participation in reclamation and drainage
rubrics_metrics.description: States may and do carry out reclamation and drainage operations (examples: Idaho's massive irrigation canals and storage reservoirs; Utah financing reclamation projects; Missouri and Florida large drainage; New Jersey ditching and filling marsh lands).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State governments are legitimate actors for reclamation and flood control; they can contract for construction and finance projects to render lands arable and control flood waters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonrenewable minerals require conservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Minerals (coal, iron, natural gas) cannot be renewed; proper use and conservation are imperative given finite supplies (e.g., original coal heritage estimated ~2.5 trillion tons; estimates of coal/iron exhaustion vary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy should treat mineral resources as finite, planning for future generations and preventing needless waste; anticipate discovery of new deposits but plan conservatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce wasteful mining methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Wasteful mining practices leave from 40% to 70% of coal in the mines, much beyond recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt improved mining methods and regulations to reduce in-mine waste; monitor industry practices to increase recoverable yields and avoid permanent loss of resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve combustion and utilization efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Imperfect combustion methods result in enormous loss of potential energy of coal (estimated ~90% is wasted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage technological improvements and standards for combustion and energy use to capture a larger fraction of coal's potential energy; public policy should promote efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent waste of natural gas by statute
rubrics_metrics.description: Unnecessary waste of natural gas occurs through uncontrolled wells and leaking pipelines (about 1,000,000,000 cubic feet lost daily); Indiana passed a statute prohibiting waste through negligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States producing gas should enact statutes to prohibit negligent waste and require maintenance and control of wells and pipelines; other gas-producing states should follow Indiana's example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect mineral lands on public domain by withdrawal and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal mineral land on the public domain can be protected without violating private-rights principles by withdrawing lands from entry and sale and properly classifying them, then providing for their right use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First withdraw public mineral lands from entry/sale; classify according to use/protection needs; then adopt policies (leasing, management) to ensure right use and prevent exploitation or waste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate disposal of surface and mineral rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Law of June 22, 1910, permitted separation of the surface of coal lands fit for agriculture from rights to the minerals beneath the surface, allowing separate disposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate surface (agricultural) and subsurface (mineral) rights to allow appropriate disposition and conservation of each resource; use legal instruments to prevent loss of agricultural land value when minerals are disposed of.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential authority to withdraw lands for public purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Law of June 25, 1910, authorized the President to withdraw lands in the United States and Alaska 'for water-power sites, irrigation, classification of lands, or other public purposes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use executive withdrawal powers to protect sites of public importance (water-power, irrigation, classification) from private entry or sale when necessary for conservation and public use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forests provide essential environmental services and must be conserved
rubrics_metrics.description: Forests are valuable directly (lumber) and indirectly for preservation of soil, water power, and waterways — they absorb moisture, prevent soil waste, check floods, regulate stream flow and maintain navigability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conservation of forests is necessary to sustain soil fertility and water resources; policy should account for indirect services beyond timber production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent forest waste: fires, reckless cutting, destructive lumbering
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary causes of forest waste include forest fires (largely from carelessness), reckless cutting of young trees, and destructive lumbering practices leaving about 20% of low-grade logs to rot or burn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement efficient government supervision to prevent fires, regulate cutting practices to protect young growth, and reform lumbering methods to reduce waste (e.g., require salvage of low-grade logs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal stewardship of public forests (withdrawal into National Forests and management)
rubrics_metrics.description: Large tracts of forest lands have been withdrawn from entry and erected into National Forests under the Forest Service (Dept. of Agriculture); these forests cannot be indiscriminately cut and are cultivated and cared for; Forest Service helps prevent fires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use withdrawal and federal management (National Forests and Forest Service) to secure long-term conservation, proper cultivation, and active fire prevention; favor administrative oversight over indiscriminate private disposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeal exploitative land-disposal statutes (timber and stone acts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Timber and stone acts resulted in public timber lands being sold cheaply (e.g., 5,000,000 acres sold 1901–1906 at $2.50/acre) and in frauds and monopolistic control; repeal of these acts is urged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate statutory frameworks that permit undervalue sale or fraud in disposal of public forest lands; replace with leasing, reservation, or managed sale policies that reflect true land value and conservation goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal purchase of watershed lands and federal-state cooperation for forest protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Appalachian Forest Reserve law (1911) provided funds 'for the purchase of land for national forests on the watersheds of navigable streams' and provided for cooperation between federal and state governments in protecting forests from fires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorize federal purchase of critical watershed lands to protect navigable streams and promote cooperative federal-state programs for fire protection and reforestation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent private monopolization of water-power sites; withdraw sites from entry
rubrics_metrics.description: Government should prevent water-power sites from getting into hands of private monopolies by withdrawing sites on the public domain from entry (already partially done) and providing for their proper use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and withdraw strategic water-power sites from private appropriation; reserve them for public interest to avoid monopolistic control and ensure equitable development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve land title and grant development rights for term-limited leases with proper fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Government should cease granting water rights in perpetuity; instead reserve title to lands and grant the right to develop and use the power for a term of years, charging a proper fee; rentals should be proportioned to true values (President Roosevelt's doctrine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt term-limited development leases rather than perpetual grants; price privileges (rents/fees) according to true value to prevent undervalued transfers and to allow public benefit capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public development of water power for comprehensive, long-term public benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: The government is better qualified than private parties to develop power resources comprehensively and coordinately with aim at ultimate development rather than immediate profits; properly managed public projects should yield revenues for social purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor coordinated public development of major power resources to achieve comprehensive benefits, flood mitigation, navigation improvements, and revenue for social programs, rather than fragmented private exploitation for short-term profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: State investigation and development of water-powers with ownership/leasing options
rubrics_metrics.description: States (e.g., New York, Wisconsin) can critically investigate water-powers, construct reservoirs (state to own reservoirs and lease power to highest bidder) or allow private construction under state supervision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage state-level studies and public projects; states may own infrastructure and lease rights, or regulate private development through supervision to secure public interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent national plan for waterways; avoid desultory local projects and log-rolling
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress historically funded waterways desultorily and unsystematically, favoring local and selfish interests; little lasting value is accomplished without a permanent plan that disregards purely local projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate a continuous, national waterways plan prioritizing projects with broad national value; avoid piecemeal, locally motivated appropriations and log-rolling that waste funds on low-value local projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finance waterways by permanent fund and apply beneficiary-pay principle
rubrics_metrics.description: To finance large waterways enterprises it has been suggested to create a permanent fund by the sale of bonds (so work is not dependent on each Congress). President Roosevelt proposed that beneficiaries where abutting land is markedly benefited should pay a portion of the expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish durable financing mechanisms (bond-funded permanent funds) for large infrastructure and apply cost-sharing so that direct beneficiaries contribute a fair share of project costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional power and flexibility in territorial governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress governs federal territory under the constitutional clause giving it power to 'dispose of and make all needful rules and regulations respecting the territory or other property belonging to the United States.' Territories may be subject to forms of government established by Congress, subject to constitutional limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress has broad authority to legislate for territories and may establish varying forms of government tailored to local circumstances, though the courts will review conflicts with constitutional provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional application to territories determined by Insular Cases (fundamental vs formal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supreme Court Insular Cases held that the Constitution may be divided into fundamental and formal parts; only fundamental parts control federal authorities in territorial government, and the Court will decide, case-by-case, which provisions are fundamental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that not all constitutional provisions automatically apply in territories; legal doctrine distinguishes fundamental protections that do apply from formal provisions that may not, with the judiciary adjudicating specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical policy for staged territorial self-government
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical practice (e.g., Northwest Ordinance): initial territorial governance by Congress-appointed governor/secretary/judges with property qualifications; when population thresholds are met (e.g., 5,000 free male inhabitants), representative assemblies and further self-government may be instituted; full autonomy granted gradually as territories settle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use staged political development tied to population and institutional capacity when transitioning territories toward self-government; maintain federal oversight initially while providing milestones for representative institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial administrative practices and safeguards (Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alaska: evolved from direct federal rule to elected legislature (1912 law), with governor appointed by President; advocates urge conservation of resources and government ownership of railways to avoid monopoly. Hawaii: organic act (1900) created territorial government, extended applicable federal laws, conferred American citizenship on prior Hawaiian citizens, set voter qualifications (male, 21, 1-year resident, able to read/write/speak English or Hawaiian). Puerto Rico: organic act (1900) created civil government, inhabitants deemed citizens of Puerto Rico (not U.S. citizens), governor and executive officers appointed by President, legislature with executive council containing appointed U.S. citizens and native members, and statutory resolution for budget deadlocks (continue prior year's arrangements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design organic acts and territorial constitutions to balance appointed and elected officials, protect local representation, set clear citizenship/voting qualifications tailored to local conditions, and include procedural safeguards (e.g., budget continuity rules) to resolve institutional disputes.
